did_you_know.text: The chapter opens with a prophecy against Moab and lists Moabite cities that were struck, including Nebo and Kiriathaim. From the outset, it emphasizes shame, captivity, and the destruction of fortresses.

The prophecy presents Chemosh, the god associated with Moab, as going into exile along with his priests and officials. This describes not only political ruin but also the collapse of Moab’s religious security.

Moab is compared to wine that has not been poured from one vessel to another or gone into exile, so its flavor and aroma have remained unchanged. The image portrays a people who lived at ease and had not experienced prolonged upheaval—but that very complacency is about to change.

The prophecy reverses the image of the wine: in the future, those who will empty Moab’s vessels and smash its jars will come. This portrays the thorough destruction of its wealth, stability, and standing.

Moab will be ashamed of Chemosh, just as the house of Israel was ashamed of Bethel, which had once been its place of confidence. The comparison highlights the disappointment of trusting in a religious refuge that cannot save in the day of judgment.

The chapter lists many Moabite cities upon which judgment came, including Holon, Jahzah, Dibon, Nebo, Beth-diblathaim, and Beth-meon. The list creates the sense that the disaster encompasses the entire land.

The prophet returns several times to Moab’s pride: its arrogance, haughtiness, conceit, and lofty heart. According to the text, pride is not merely a character trait but a central cause of the judgment brought upon Moab.

Alongside the words of rebuke, a personal lament is heard: the prophet says that he wails and weeps for Moab. The chapter therefore presents both judgment for sin and grief over the suffering and destruction.

The verse uses a sequence of images—terror, a pit, and a snare—to describe a situation in which the fugitives can find no escape: whoever flees from terror falls into a pit, and whoever climbs out of the pit is caught in a snare.

Despite the severe description of destruction, the chapter ends with a promise: in the latter days, Moab’s fortunes will be restored. The ending adds a dimension of future hope to the prophecy rather than leaving it solely as a description of ruin.
